lead: Wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) sends several light signals through one fiber at the same time, each on its own wavelength. One laser and its modulator give only a few Gb/s, while the 1550 nm window holds several THz of usable bandwidth. WDM uses that window as many separate channels, so capacity grows with the number of channels N, not with electronic speed. Telephone backbones, cable TV feeds and data-centre links use it.
prereq: You need: single-mode fiber and its low-loss 1550 nm window (see Single-mode and multimode fibers; cutoff wavelength) and the laser transmitter (see Semiconductor laser diodes).

sections.h3: Why one fiber carries many colours

blocks.text: WDM gives each signal a different wavelength λ. One wavelength with its own data is called a channel, and all channels share one fiber. If there are N channels and each carries B bit/s, the total capacity is C = N × B, as long as the amplifiers, filters and receivers allow it.

blocks.where: C is the total bit rate in bit/s; N is the number of wavelength channels; B is the bit rate of one channel in bit/s.

blocks.text: Channel spacing can be given in frequency (GHz) or in wavelength (nm). Since f = c/λ, a small step in frequency Δf matches a small step in wavelength Δλ:
Δλ = λ²Δf / c  and  Δf = cΔλ / λ²
blocks.where: Δλ is the spacing in wavelength (m); λ is the operating wavelength (m); Δf is the spacing in frequency (Hz); c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum.

blocks.text: At 1550 nm a 100 GHz step is 0.80 nm. The same 100 GHz step is 0.57 nm at 1310 nm and 0.86 nm at 1610 nm, because Δλ grows as λ². The ITU-T DWDM grid (G.694.1) anchors channels at 193.1 THz and steps in 100 GHz, 50 GHz or finer slots; dense WDM (DWDM) uses these tight spacings with temperature-controlled lasers. Coarse WDM (CWDM, G.694.2) uses 20 nm spacing: 18 channels from 1270 nm to 1610 nm, uncooled lasers and short reach.

A multiplexer combines λ<sub>1</sub>…λ<sub>N</sub> into one fiber; a demultiplexer separates them. Some syllabi say “wavelength multiplexer” or “WDM mux/demux” for the same pair. Five common parts do this job.

items: Prism: the refraction angle changes with wavelength; simple, few channels.
Diffraction grating: periodic grooves send each wavelength to a different angle; good for many channels.
Thin-film dielectric filter: a stack of layers passes one band and reflects the rest; used in mux/demux and add/drop.
Arrayed waveguide grating (AWG): waveguides with fixed path differences interfere so each wavelength focuses on a different output; common in integrated optics.
Fiber Bragg grating (FBG): a periodic index pattern in the fiber reflects one wavelength and passes the rest.

blocks.text: Four numbers describe a mux or demux. Insertion loss is the drop in dB from the input to the wanted output; lower is better. Adjacent-channel crosstalk is 10 log₁₀(leaked power from the next channel ÷ wanted channel power); the leak is smaller than the wanted power, so the value is negative, and more negative is better. Channel uniformity is the spread in dB between the strongest and weakest output. Passband width is the range of wavelengths over which the loss stays low. The couplers and gratings inside these parts are in Passive devices.

The comb is the set of channel frequencies. From the first channel centre to the last it is (N − 1)Δf wide, not NΔf, because N channels have N − 1 gaps. When a question asks how many channels fit in a band, divide the band by the spacing: each channel takes one slot of width Δf.

Capacity grows with N, but N is limited by the amplifier gain band (the erbium C-band is about 1530 to 1565 nm, see Optical amplifiers), laser wavelength drift, filter passband and crosstalk. A mux with 1.5 dB insertion loss removes 1.5 dB from every channel, and the demux at the far end removes its own share. The passband must cover laser drift and modulation chirp, and the crosstalk sets how close the channels can sit. In a network each channel becomes a lightpath, see Optical network concepts.

examples.question: A DWDM system uses 40 channels on the ITU grid near 1550 nm, spaced 100 GHz apart, each carrying 10 Gb/s. (a) Find the total capacity. (b) Find the spacing in nanometres. (c) Find the width of the comb from the first to the last channel centre. (d) The erbium C-band runs from 1530 nm to 1565 nm. How many 100 GHz slots does it hold, and what capacity is that at 10 Gb/s per channel?
steps: N = 40 channels and B = 10 Gb/s per channel. Total capacity C = N × B = 40 × 10 = 400 Gb/s.
The comb has N − 1 = 39 gaps: width = 39 × 100 GHz = 3.9 THz, or 39 × 0.8008 = 31.23 nm.
Band edges in frequency: f = c/λ. At 1530 nm, f = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ (1530 × 10⁻⁹) = 196.08 THz; at 1565 nm, f = 191.69 THz. Band width = 196.08 − 191.69 = 4.385 THz.
Slots = 4.385 THz ÷ 0.1 THz = 43.85, so 43 whole slots. Capacity = 43 × 10 = 430 Gb/s.
Check: 35 nm ÷ 0.80 nm per slot ≈ 43.7, which also gives 43 whole slots.
examples.answer: (a) 400 Gb/s. (b) 0.8008 nm. (c) 3.9 THz, or 31.23 nm. (d) The C-band is 4.385 THz wide and holds 43 slots of 100 GHz, which is 430 Gb/s at 10 Gb/s per channel.

traps: 100 GHz is not always 0.8 nm: Δλ = λ²Δf/c, so the same frequency spacing is 0.57 nm at 1310 nm and 0.86 nm at 1610 nm.
Comb width uses N − 1 gaps; the number of channels in a band uses band ÷ spacing. Mixing the two gives answers off by one channel.
Total capacity is N × B in each direction. Multiply by 2 only when the question counts both directions of a duplex pair.
CWDM is 20 nm spacing over 1270 to 1610 nm; DWDM is 100 GHz, 50 GHz or finer. Do not mix the names.
Crosstalk is a negative dB ratio, so −30 dB is better than −20 dB. Insertion loss is a positive dB number.

quiz.a: One wavelength that carries its own independent data signal through the shared fiber.

quiz.q: State the ITU-T DWDM anchor frequency and two common channel spacings.
quiz.a: Anchor 193.1 THz; common spacings 100 GHz and 50 GHz.

quiz.q: Why does WDM raise capacity without faster electronics?
quiz.a: It adds parallel wavelength channels, each running at the electronic bit rate B, so the total capacity is N × B while each transmitter and receiver stays at B.

quiz.q: A link has 32 WDM channels, each at 10 Gb/s. Find the total capacity.
Find Δλ for 50 GHz spacing at 1550 nm, and the frequency spacing that matches 0.4 nm at 1550 nm.
A CWDM system uses 20 nm spacing near 1550 nm. Express this spacing in THz.
quiz.a: Δf = cΔλ/λ² = 3 × 10⁸ × 20 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ (2.4025 × 10⁻¹²) = 2.50 × 10¹² Hz = 2.50 THz, which is 25 DWDM slots of 100 GHz.

quiz.q: A mux has −25 dB adjacent-channel crosstalk and 1.5 dB insertion loss. What fraction of the next channel leaks in, and what fraction of the wanted power gets through?
quiz.a: Crosstalk: 10<sup>−2.5</sup> = 0.0032, so the leak is 0.32 percent of the wanted power. Insertion loss: 10<sup>−0.15</sup> = 0.708, so 70.8 percent of the wanted power reaches the output. A −30 dB part would leak only 0.10 percent.

quiz.q: Why can a 100 GHz grid not be described as a fixed 0.8 nm spacing from 1270 nm to 1610 nm?
quiz.a: Because Δλ = λ²Δf/c changes with λ². For 100 GHz it is 0.54 nm at 1270 nm, 0.80 nm at 1550 nm and 0.86 nm at 1610 nm. The grid is fixed in frequency, not in wavelength.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use flexible-grid ROADMs, where a channel takes as many 12.5 GHz slices as it needs, coherent 400G and 800G channels, and the L-band beyond 1570 nm. Research moves to space-division multiplexing, where several cores or modes share one fiber. Search terms: ITU-T G.694.1, CWDM grid, AWG, ROADM, flex grid.

figure.caption: Forty 10 Gb/s channels, 100 GHz (0.80 nm) apart, are combined on one fiber for 400 Gb/s. From λ1 to λ40 the comb spans 39 gaps, 3.9 THz or 31.2 nm, and it fits inside the 4.385 THz erbium C-band, which has room for 43 such slots.
